pinterest.title: Filipino Wedding Traditions: Sponsors, Coins, Veil and Cord Explained
pinterest.description: A guide to Filipino wedding traditions grouped by when they happen: the pamamanhikan before the day, the arras, candle, veil and cord rites in the ceremony, and the money dance at the reception. Learn who the ninong and ninang are, what secondary sponsors do, and why it helps to ask each side of the family which customs they keep. Includes notes for Australians marrying in the Philippines.

pinterest.title: The Arras: What the 13 Coins Mean in Filipino Wedding Traditions
pinterest.description: The arras is often described as a set of 13 coins that passes between the couple during a Filipino wedding ceremony. The coins are often told to stand for provision and a shared household. Who hands them to whom differs between parishes and families, so ask your officiant how they run it. Read the full guide to Filipino wedding customs, from sponsors to the money dance.

pinterest.title: Veil and Cord Rites: A Filipino Wedding Ceremony Guide
pinterest.description: In many Filipino wedding ceremonies, veil sponsors drape a veil over the bride's head and the groom's shoulders, and cord sponsors then place a cord, sometimes called a yugal, often in a loose figure eight. The veil is often told to show the couple clothed as one, and the cord the lasting bond of marriage. Philippine law requires no religious rite, so these can sit in a civil or celebrant-led ceremony too.

slides: Filipino wedding traditions you might not know, and what each one is often told to mean
Before the day: the pamamanhikan. The groom and his parents call on the bride's parents to ask for her hand and their blessing. The date is often settled here.
The sponsors. Principal sponsors, the ninong and ninang, stand with the couple. Secondary sponsors, often in pairs, light the candles, place the veil and place the cord.
The arras. 13 coins pass between the couple during the ceremony, often told to stand for provision and a shared household.
The veil and cord. A veil over the bride's head and the groom's shoulders, then a cord, the yugal, often in a loose figure eight. Often told to stand for the lasting bond of marriage.
The money dance. Guests often pin notes to the couple's clothes as cash gifts. There is no set amount, and no guest should feel obliged to join.
What to wear. A barong tagalog, an embroidered shirt, for the groom. Filipiniana, a broad name for traditional Filipino dress, for the bride.

instagram_carousel.caption:
Who are the ninong and ninang? What happens with the coins? Does the cord go on before or after the veil?

Filipino wedding traditions are rarely written down in one place, and many families hold their own version. Our new guide groups common customs by when they happen: the pamamanhikan before the day, the arras, candle, veil and cord rites in the ceremony, and the money dance at the reception.

One thing to hold on to: these customs vary by family, faith and region. The most useful step is also the simplest. Ask each side of the family which customs they keep and what they mean to them.

Philippine law needs no religious rite, so many couples keep the arras, veil and cord as cultural moments in a civil or celebrant-led ceremony, wherever they marry.

You do not need to keep every custom. Many couples choose a handful that mean something to their families and let the rest go gently.

Read the full guide via the link in our bio, or send us a message to chat with a Wedded Advisor about your celebration.

newsletter.subject: Filipino wedding traditions, explained by moment
newsletter.preview: Sponsors, the 13 coins, the veil and cord, the money dance, and what Australians should know about marrying.
newsletter.blurb: If one of you has a Filipino parent or grandparent, the questions tend to arrive early. Who are the ninong and ninang? What happens with the coins? Our new guide groups Filipino wedding customs by when they happen, explains who does what, and is careful about what is documented and what is only often told. It also covers the official paperwork steps for Australians marrying in the Philippines, and how to register your marriage back home.
